title: egress h2 alpn downgrade investigation
content:
Quick scratchpad for the odd case where clients fall back from h2->http/1.1 intermittently after VPC peering path changes. Mix of commands, raw outputs, hypotheses and next steps. Notes to self - informal.

Summary of the symptom:
- From customer VPC (peered) some requests to host api.redwood-private.example.com negotiate h2; others drop to http/1.1. When http/1.1 is used, we see higher latency and tokenization failures for streaming.
- Issue appears after peering route change (route table update datestamped ~2025-11-02 03:14 UTC).
- Affected only through peering path (not public internet) and only for a handful of client IPs in 10.32.128.0/24.
- TLS completes but ALPN advertised in ClientHello sometimes not picked up / peer responds with no h2 in ServerHello.

What I've tried (raw commands + notable outputs):

1) curl client-side checks
$ curl -v --http2 https://api.redwood-private.example.com/health -H "Host: api.redwood-private.example.com" --resolve api.redwood-private.example.com:443:10.1.5.12
* About to connect() to 10.1.5.12 port 443
* Connected to 10.1.5.12 (10.1.5.12) port 443 (#0)
* ALPN, offering h2
* successfully set certificate verify locations:
 ...
* TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, Finished
* SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
* Server did not agree to use h2
> GET /health HTTP/1.1
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK

- Same curl against public IP (nat path) consistently shows "ALPN, server accepted h2". So server is capable. Problem is path/peer.

2) openssl s_client to capture ClientHello and ServerHello ALPN fields
$ openssl s_client -connect 10.1.5.12:443 -alpn h2 -msg -tls1_3 < /dev/null 2>&1 | sed -n '1,120p'
>>> TLS 1.3 Handshake [length 0005]
    01 00 00 2c 03 03 58 ...
ClientHello, <length>
    (advertised ALPN: h2,http/1.1)
<<< TLS 1.3 Handshake
ServerHello, <length>
    (no alpn extension)

- On bad path ServerHello missing alpn extension. On good path ServerHello contains alpn=h2.

3) tcpdump / tshark captures (client-side and server-side)
Client side (10.32.128.37 -> 10.1.5.12):
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.1.5.12 and port 443 -w /tmp/ct1.pcap
- Reconstructed ClientHello shows ALPN h2 present.
Server side capture (on private node behind peering):
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth1 host 10.32.128.37 and port 443 -w /tmp/st1.pcap
- Server sees ClientHello, but response path shows ServerHello without ALPN.
- Observed occasional TCP retransmits and one instance of duplicated SYN-ACK in the trace (possible middlebox interference).

4) packet sizes / MTU suspicion
- ClientHello size ~ 1.2KB (multiple extensions). Several middleboxes on peered route are known to rewrite/fragment packets.
- I forced smaller TLS ClientHello by disabling some extensions client-side (curl can't easily do this). Experimented with openssl to reduce to minimal; when ClientHello bytes < 900 bytes, ServerHello comes back with ALPN reliably.

5) ALPN probe using socat (raw TLS handshake control)
$ echo | socat - OPENSSL:10.1.5.12:443,verify=0,alpn=h2
- Succeeds on good path; on bad path socat completes TLS but server does not select h2.

6) DNS / SNI checks
- Verified host header and SNI consistently set to api.redwood-private.example.com.
- No wildcard/redirects.

Hypotheses:
- Middlebox on peered route is rewriting/stripping extensions above some packet size threshold -> ALPN extension lost in transit when ClientHello larger than threshold. This explains packet-size correlation.
- Asymmetric path with different egress NAT -> TLS handshake traverses different middlebox on return (server->client) that fails to forward alpn extension.
- Some intermediate device (firewall, IPS) terminating TLS early or doing TLS inspection but rewrapped without ALPN.
- Kernel-level TCP offload / MSS clamping on route causing fragmentation leading to extension truncation.

Evidence for/against:
- For: smaller ClientHello => h2 selected. ServerHello missing ALPN only on bad path. Public path works fine.
- Against: We see TLS Finished and app data in both cases; if an inline TLS terminator were rewrapping they'd likely offer h2. Hard to be certain.

Quick experiments to reproduce / confirm:
- Recreate large ClientHello: add dummy extensions from client to exceed MTU and verify ServerHello drop. Done, reproduces.
- From server side, initiate connection to client (reverse) to see if alpn also stripped upstream. (TODO)
- Run MSS/DF toggles with iptables on client to force fragmentation/DF clearing.

Immediate mitigation ideas:
- Force clients to prefer http/1.1 (painful, avoid if possible).
- Use TLS session resumption with smaller CH? Not reliable.
- Adjust peering MTU/clamps to avoid fragmentation at the middlebox. Coordinate with customer network team to check for firewall/IPS devices that do TLS inspection.
- Add an edge proxy on the peered route that actively enforces ALPN/h2 by terminating TLS at an internal hop and opening a fresh connection to backend (requires trust/KMS changes).

Notes for next on-call steps:
- Collect full packet capture (pcap) on both sides simultaneously of a failing handshake (timestamps must be synced).
- Run openssl -msg -tls1_3 on both sides to show raw extension parsing.
- Ask customer networking team if any IDS/IPS updates or middlebox firmware changes were applied around 2025-11-02 03:00-04:00 UTC.
- Test with explicit MTU/MSS changes: ip link set dev eth0 mtu 1436 and 1500 to observe behavior.
- Try a controlled test where we advertise only "http/1.1" in ClientHello to see if server intentionally refuses h2 in certain conditions (server code path?).

Unresolved questions / TODO:
- Is there any per-connection policy on the server side that refuses h2 for certain source subnets? (grep config)
- Can we get kernel dmesg/syslog from the border routers for the timestamp window?
- Who applied the route update? correlate with infra gitops commit.

Raw diagnostic snippets (keep for ticket):
- openssl showing missing alpn on server hello (bad trace) excerpt:
    <<< TLS 1.3 Handshake
    ServerHello, length=...
    version: 0x303
    random: ...
    extensions: (no alpn)

- tcpdump note: saw one packet with IP "MF" bit set then not seen again (possible reassembly issue).

References / similar tickets:
- jira NET-1027 (linked) has prior note about MTU + TLS extension truncation in peered networks.
- customer thread: slack #cust-networks thread t/ALPN-oddness dated 2025-11-02.

Final thought: the size/fragmentation signal is the strongest lead. Prioritize synchronized pcap and asking the peer network team about inline TLS devices or MTU clamping rules. If confirmed, we can push a small MTU clamp on our peering interface as a temporary fix (documented rollback).

End of scratchpad.
